analysis.one_liner: Ratifies the FTC's legal authority to run the national do-not-call registry.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 63 Senate cosponsors from both parties, the bill never received a vote in the 108th Congress — but Congress had already passed companion legislation days earlier, so the do-not-call registry took effect without it.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2003 a federal court ruled that the Federal Trade Commission lacked the legal authority to run the national do-not-call registry, the list that lets people opt out of telemarketing sales calls. This bill answered that ruling by writing the FTC's authority directly into law and ratifying the registry rule the agency had already put in place. It was introduced with 63 cosponsors from both parties but never came up for a vote; other legislation passed the same week did the same job, and the registry took effect anyway.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who signed up for (or wanted to join) the national do-not-call registry. Writing the FTC's authority into law protects their sign-ups from being invalidated by court challenges to the agency's power, and keeps the federal government able to block unwanted telemarketing sales calls.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Household phone users on the do-not-call list

how_it_helps.text: It declares that the FTC is authorized under the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act to implement and enforce a national do-not-call registry, removing the legal doubt created by the court ruling.
It ratifies the do-not-call registry provision of the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, effective March 31, 2003, so consumers' existing sign-ups could not be thrown out.
It drew 63 cosponsors — 34 Democrats, 28 Republicans, and 1 Independent — including both party leaders, showing overwhelming cross-party support.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies, call centers, and list brokers, who lose access to households on the registry and face the industry-wide shift away from cold calls. Political campaigns, charities, surveys, and companies that already do business with a caller are exempt from the underlying rule, so they bear no new cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill ratifies only the FTC's registry rule; it does not address the Federal Communications Commission's parallel telemarketing rules, leaving open questions about which agency covers which kinds of calls.

It ratifies the Telemarketing Sales Rule's registry provision as written, so the rule's exemptions — calls from political campaigns, charities, surveys, and companies a person already does business with — would remain untouched.

Writing the FTC's authority into law entrenches the commission's enforcement power over the telemarketing industry without adding new consumer protections beyond what the existing rule already provides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was large and immediate for consumers: the registry covered tens of millions of households and gave people a simple, free way to stop sales calls, at a modest cost to a telemarketing industry built around unwanted calling. The bill's actual design was narrow and sensible — it did one thing, writing the FTC's authority into law to protect the registry from court challenges — but it left gaps: it ratified the rule as written, so political calls, charities, surveys, and companies a consumer already does business with could still call, and it addressed only the FTC's rule, not the FCC's parallel jurisdiction. On balance the costs fell on a specific industry whose product most people were trying to avoid, while the benefit was broad consumer relief, though its incompleteness meant the phone did not go fully quiet.

outcome.mechanism: It got stuck in committee — introduced, read twice, and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended — but by then other legislation ratifying the FTC's authority had already been signed, so the registry took effect and this bill simply became redundant.

narrative.text: Senator Ensign and 62 colleagues introduced the bill on September 25, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
The committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it; it sat in committee until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

Days after this bill was introduced, both chambers passed companion legislation ratifying the FTC's do-not-call authority, which the President signed on September 29, 2003, allowing the registry to take effect on schedule on October 1, 2003.

A federal district court had ruled in late September 2003 that the FTC lacked authority to run the registry, and a second court quickly upheld it, so the broader litigation threat that prompted the bill faded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead: although this bill itself never got a vote, Congress passed companion legislation within days and the do-not-call registry took effect on schedule, so its death cost the public nothing. Telemarketers' legal challenge was overridden either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, since the registry took effect anyway

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill ratifying the FTC's authority to run the do-not-call registry.

for.name: 28 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Majority Leader Frist and other party leaders.

against.name: Telemarketing industry plaintiffs (including the American Teleservices Association)
against.role: Industry plaintiffs in Mainstream Marketing Services v. FTC
against.what_they_did: Sued in federal court to block the do-not-call registry, winning a ruling that the FTC lacked authority — the ruling this bill was drafted to override.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan — 34 Democrats, 28 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsored, including the majority and minority leaders — and no senator is on record opposing it.

industries.note: A ratified, legally secure do-not-call registry lets millions of households bar sales calls, shrinking the pool of people telemarketers can legally dial. The industry fought the registry in court, and the bill was written to take that fight off the table.
The registry reduces the value of consumer phone lists for outbound sales campaigns. Firms that sell and rent phone lists lose inventory when households opt out.

The bill writes the FTC's authority to run the registry directly into law, cementing its role as the enforcer of telemarketing rules against future court challenges. This strengthens the agency's consumer-protection mandate rather than weakening it.
